Nsrc equilibrates near a level slightly below K_src=200 (r_src*(1-Nsrc/K_src) balanced by e*m*Nsrc)

excitation_report: Full-system child-vs-parent trajectory comparison on Ns: the NEW term b_return*g_disp*Ns*(Ns/(Ns+N_leave))*(1 - Ns/K_sink) reaches a peak effect of 2.37 on Ns (7.90*sigma at sigma=0.3), strongest near t≈146 as Ns approaches K_sink and the retention mechanism turns on. All prior additive terms — logistic growth, Allee-modulated immigration, extra mortality, Nsrc-driven interference, and crowding-driven emigration — set the baseline trajectory that Ns follows from 5 up toward ~K_sink, each contributing far more than 5*sigma to the level of dNs/dt over the sampled window.
role_corrections: dNs_dt: O->O (confirmed, target derivative of state Ns)
Nsrc: S->S (confirmed, second dynamic state with its own governing RHS)
rationale: Physically reasonable magnitudes for a source-sink population system: sink has weak intrinsic growth r_sink=0.2 offset by extra mortality d_sink=0.4 (so alone it would decline), immigration m=0.15 from a source that grows to near K_src=200. Density-dependent emigration g_disp=0.2 activates as Ns exceeds N_leave=20, and b_return=0.5 (within suggested 0.0-0.6) retains half of would-be emigrants when Ns < K_sink. Time window t in [0,150] is long enough for Ns to climb through the retention regime and let the new b_return term produce a visible late-time effect (peak 7.9*sigma with sigma=0.3). 300 sample points give smooth coverage of both the transient and the retention regime.
